description:
We're two AI Master's students at BTU Cottbus, Mohammedzaid and Ananya, and we build AI-first: problems where ML does the real work, not a chatbot bolted on.
What we bring: Python, ML and deep learning, time-series analysis, geospatial AI and LLMs/agents, plus the math underneath (stats, probability, linear algebra), so we can tell a real result from noise.
summary: FlameScope turns NASA's microgravity combustion archive into fire-safety answers for spacecraft and Moon bases. It answers plain-English questions with NASA's own words from 19 investigations, linked to their DOIs, and checks every number before showing an AI summary. From the BASS-II space-station experiment we built a flame map from 408 labeled airflow steps: acrylic stopped burning between 13.6% and 14.6% oxygen. A 30% Moon base lies far beyond anything tested, and FlameScope says so.
details:
FlameScope is a web dashboard that answers fire-safety questions for spacecraft, space stations, Moon bases and rovers using NASA's own microgravity combustion research. We turned 19 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive into 7,770 searchable passages. Users ask questions in plain English and get NASA's own text, linked to the source page and DOI. A local AI model adds a short summary, and a checker withholds it unless every number and citation appears in NASA's text.

The BASS-II space-station experiment recorded flame outcomes only in operators' notes, so we parsed them into 408 labeled airflow steps. Our flame map shows that acrylic stopped burning between 13.6% and 14.6% oxygen in microgravity, compared with 14–15% on Earth. Planned Moon habitats at 30% oxygen lie far beyond anything NASA tested, and FlameScope says so clearly instead of guessing. A research map ranks the 19 investigations for each habitat type.

Benefits and impact: cited answers in seconds instead of hours of searching, and a clear view of what NASA has and has not measured. This helps designers choose materials, smoke detectors and suppression systems for future habitats.

Tools: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Ollama with the open Qwen2.5 model; sentence-transformers, scikit-learn, pandas and SciPy; GitHub Pages. Everything runs on a laptop with no API key.

Creativity and key factors: NASA's words come first; the AI is checked, not trusted; and "no data" is a valid answer. We favored accuracy over looking impressive. For example, we removed three AI answers that misread NASA's text, and we state every limitation on the site.
dataRefs: NASA NTRS: Marcum, Olson & Ferkul (2016), normal-gravity vs microgravity blowoff limits\thttps://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20160012691
